tldr: The authors propose phi-RIE, a framework that converts selected objects from a photorealistically reconstructed 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene into independent, movable simulator assets while seamlessly completing occluded backgrounds. By coupling object generation/alignment with background removal/completion, phi-RIE enables accurate and artifact-free interactive environment construction across large-scale tests on 50 scenes and robot manipulation tasks.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline and key components of the system. From camera views and the Gaussian scene, object masks and observed surfaces are extracted (Scene Observation). Assets are aligned while the background is removed and completed in tandem (Coupled Scene Construction), enabling an Interactive Environment where Gaussians render aligned with physics engine poses.
overview:
Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) allow us to reconstruct complex real-world rooms and cluttered tabletops with incredible detail. However, bringing these Gaussian scenes directly into robot simulators does not enable physical interaction. 3DGS is fundamentally just an ensemble of points optimized to reproduce captured camera views. As a result, boundaries between objects and tables remain entangled, and unobserved geometry—like the underside of an object or the hidden surface beneath it—is entirely missing.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed phi-RIE, a pipeline that transforms selected objects into physically interactive simulator assets while preserving the beautiful appearance of the remaining Gaussians. The core idea is coupling asset construction directly with source removal and background completion. Using a single object identity, generative AI completes the object's unobserved shape and registers it at true scale. At the same time, this shape information guides the clean carving away of the original scene Gaussians and the inpainting of newly exposed planar surfaces like tabletops.

Evaluations span large-scale geometric and visual assessments across 50 ScanNet++ scenes (1,871 object conversion requests) alongside robot manipulation experiments in RoboCasa. The results show that evidence-based selection from multiple generators and registration retries significantly improve geometric asset alignment, while also yielding substantial manipulation gains over a single-generator baseline.
contributions: Established a pipeline that converts selected objects into independently movable Gaussian simulator assets while preserving the high-fidelity appearance of unedited regions.
Proposed Coupled Scene Construction, which links candidate asset alignment and selection with Gaussian removal and background inpainting using shared object instance information.

Systematically validated the approach across multiple stages: geometric accuracy and visual cost across 50 ScanNet++ scenes, physical plausibility checks, and real manipulation policy executions in RoboCasa.

sections.heading: Why Can't Photorealistic 3D Scans Just Move in a Simulator?
sections.summary: While 3DGS excels at photorealistic scene capture, it lacks object separation, unobserved shape completion, and visual-physical state alignment needed for physics simulation. These challenges are coupled: adding an asset duplicates geometry, while simply removing an object leaves holes. phi-RIE resolves these issues in an integrated manner.
sections.details:
Simulation environments for robot learning require objects to carry independent identities, true-to-life scale, collision geometry, and appearances that follow physical movement. Existing benchmarks like LIBERO rely on manually curated assets. However, reproducing real-world clutter and natural arrangements demands direct Real-to-Sim conversion from captured scenes.

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a promising tool due to its high visual fidelity and rendering speed. Yet, simply loading a 3DGS scene into a simulator does not even allow lifting a cup. 3DGS primitives (ellipsoids) are optimized solely to match visual appearance across camera views. Consequently, a cup and the table beneath it often share the same Gaussians, and hidden surfaces like the cup's bottom or the occluded tabletop do not exist at all.

Solving this requires satisfying three conditions simultaneously:
- Separation: Decoupling captured appearance into independently movable object entities.
- Completion: Reconstructing missing geometry for collision checking, as well as background surfaces exposed when the object moves.
- State consistency: Binding visual Gaussians to collision meshes in a unified coordinate frame so appearance tracks physical simulator states.

Leaving the original cup's Gaussians creates visual ghosting when adding a completed asset, whereas merely deleting them leaves a gaping hole in the table. phi-RIE addresses this by coupling asset creation with scene removal.

sections.heading: Where Gaussian Robotics and Real-to-Sim Stand Today
sections.summary: Research connecting Gaussians to physics simulation and Real-to-Sim pipelines is rapidly growing. However, existing methods typically render objects as standard textured meshes over Gaussian backgrounds, or rebuild the entire scene from scratch. phi-RIE sets itself apart by locally editing and completing Gaussians while maintaining native Gaussian rendering for both objects and backgrounds.
sections.details:
Related work broadly spans three main categories:

### 3DGS in Robotics
Efforts to integrate 3DGS or 2DGS into robotics simulators (such as SplatSim and DISCOVERSE) and studies embedding physical dynamics directly into Gaussians (such as PhysGaussian) are advancing quickly. However, a pipeline capable of cleanly separating movable objects from gap-free backgrounds in real scans has been lacking.

### Real-to-Sim Scene Construction
Techniques converting real video or scans into simulation environments include Re3Sim and SimFoundry. Yet, these methods often render only the background as Gaussians while replacing movable objects with textured meshes, degrading visual fidelity. Other approaches, such as GASE and SimuScene, perform image-based separation and completion, but rebuilding the entire scene introduces heavy computation and potential accuracy loss. phi-RIE is designed to locally edit existing Gaussian fields, preserving high-quality unedited regions intact.

### 3D Generation and Scene Editing AI
State-of-the-art 3D generative models like TRELLIS and ReconViaGen can produce high-quality meshes or Gaussians from single or sparse views. However, they do not handle real-scale alignment, collision models, or source removal from the original scene. phi-RIE leverages these generative backends while assembling all the missing pieces required for full simulator integration.

sections.heading: How phi-RIE Couples Asset Creation with Background Inpainting
sections.summary: phi-RIE operates in three stages: Scene Observation, Coupled Scene Construction, and Interactive Environment. Using shared object segmentation evidence, the object branch conducts candidate selection and alignment, while the background branch concurrently handles source removal and planar inpainting.
sections.details:
### III-A & III-B Scene Representation and Scene Observation
Inputs consist of an initial Gaussian reconstruction $G^0$, calibrated camera views $\mathcal{V}$, and scene surface points. First, SAM3 extracts 2D masks of target objects across multi-view images, which are projected onto 3D scene surfaces using depth rays. Aggregating these across a voxel grid yields observed surface samples $Q_i$ and spatial bounds for target object $i$.

### III-C Coupled Scene Construction
This core stage synchronizes object asset creation and background processing using shared object boundary cues:
- Object Candidate Generation and Alignment: Multiple candidate assets (mesh + Gaussians) are generated using single-view TRELLIS and multi-view ReconViaGen. Dimensions from observed surface points $Q_i$ initialize candidate scale. After searching yaw orientations under an upright assumption, a partial-to-complete ICP optimizes translation, rotation, and scale. A clipped nearest-neighbor distance suppresses outlier penalties from unobserved areas during evaluation.
- Verification, Selection, and Registration Retry: Candidates undergo sequential checks for geometric consistency, scale plausibility, collision viability, and static settling tests in simulation. If initial attempts fail, a retry mechanism tests alternate vertical orientation hypotheses.
- Source Removal: To prevent ghosting artifacts when objects move, original Gaussians are pruned using three integrated criteria: proximity to observed surfaces ($R_i^{\rm obs}$), proximity to completed asset surfaces ($R_i^{\rm asset}$), and multi-view mask voting ($R_i^{\rm mask}$).
- Background Inpainting: Regions exposed by removal are completed using texture targets generated by an image inpainting model. Normal-aligned Gaussian disks are initialized on local supporting planes and optimized. Existing background Gaussians remain fixed, optimizing only newly added fill Gaussians $G^{\rm fill}$ for clean completion.

### III-D Interactive Environment
Physics engines (MuJoCo or PyBullet) compute rigid-body dynamics using convex decomposition meshes produced via CoACD. Simulator-derived rigid transformations $T_i(t)$ are applied analytically to the Gaussian centers and covariance matrices. As objects roll or lift, their photorealistic appearance tracks physical motion identically. An optional DiffusionHarmonizer can also be applied post-rendering to reconcile dynamic shadows and lighting changes.

captions.F2: Overall architecture of the method. Using masks and surface data from Scene Observation, the top object branch handles asset generation, alignment, and selection, while the bottom background branch removes and completes source Gaussians. The right side illustrates how converted assets render dynamically following simulator physics poses.

sections.heading: From Geometry to Manipulation: Evaluating 50 Real-World Scenes
sections.summary: phi-RIE was evaluated on 1,871 object conversion tasks across 50 ScanNet++ scenes and in RoboCasa manipulation trials. Registration retries and candidate selection improved geometric F1 score from 0.336 to 0.383, while robot manipulation success rates increased by 11.46 points over a single-generator baseline.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Quantitative Scene Construction and Physical Plausibility
Performance was evaluated across 1,871 object conversion requests in 50 ScanNet++ scenes.
- Geometric Accuracy and Alignment: Selecting from a candidate pool of TRELLIS and ReconViaGen using evidence raised the F1 score at a 20 mm threshold from 0.336 to 0.348, and adding vertical retry raised it to 0.383. Compared to fixed prioritization (defaulting to ReconViaGen), Chamfer Distance (CD) dropped by 25.1%. However, retries increased scene construction time from 35.68 minutes to 70.82 minutes.
- Visual Trade-offs: Evaluating initial rendering quality after object replacement and background completion showed a modest PSNR drop of just 1.144 dB, retaining high visual fidelity.
- Robot Manipulation Tasks (RoboCasa): Across three task families (480 total trials), phi-RIE achieved 128/480 successes (26.7%), an 11.46-point gain over the single-generator baseline (TRELLIS only, 73/480, 15.2%). While below the pristine reference environment (385/480), this demonstrates that delivering executable assets directly improves manipulation policy success.

### IV-C Qualitative Results
Each pipeline stage (original Gaussians -> source removal -> background inpainting -> placement of physics-ready asset) executes cleanly. Across actions such as flipping a cup, pushing a keyboard, or applying impulsive forces that send objects flying, rigid collision meshes and Gaussian renderings remain tightly coupled.

### IV-D Ablation Studies
- Generative Backends: Comparing TRELLIS, TRELLIS.2, SAM 3D Objects, and ReconViaGen revealed trade-offs: TRELLIS excelled in geometric accuracy, whereas SAM 3D Objects showed higher settling stability in simulation (16/29). No single generator dominated all metrics, validating the multi-generator pool design.
- Input Requirements: Replacing laser scan meshes with surface points fused directly from rendered Gaussian depths resulted in only a minor F1 score drop from 0.582 to 0.553 under automatic detection. This confirms practical environments can be constructed without external mesh scans.

captions.F4: Robot manipulation within the constructed interactive environments. Across flipping a cup (top), moving a keyboard (middle), and shifting headphones (bottom), Gaussian appearance tracks simulator physical states without visual breakdown.
captions.F5: Impulse interaction tests in simulation. As the cup and headphones tumble and translate under physics engine dynamics, they move cleanly as independent entities without visual artifacts.
captions.F6: Comparison of post-render Appearance Harmonization. Applying DiffusionHarmonizer effectively softens unnatural shadows and inconsistent lighting after object movement.

sections.heading: Takeaway: Turning Static Scans into Interactive Playgrounds
sections.summary: phi-RIE opens the door to turning photorealistic 3DGS scans into interactive simulation environments by coupling object generation with background completion. Demonstrating gains in both geometric precision and robotic manipulation, it marks an important step forward for Real-to-Sim research.
sections.details:
This work introduces phi-RIE, a pipeline that converts selected objects from captured 3D Gaussian scenes into independently movable physical assets while preserving the photorealistic appearance of unedited regions.

Tightly coupling object generation with background removal and inpainting through shared evidence—and driving Gaussians with rigid-body simulation poses—creates environments where visual and physical states stay aligned. Experiments quantitatively show improvements in geometric alignment, higher manipulation task success over single-generator baselines, and modest visual conversion costs.

As a result, real-world Gaussian scans are no longer restricted to static visualization. They can now serve as interactive testbeds where robots physically interact and learn through trial and error.

takeaways: When converting 3DGS scenes into simulators, coupling asset generation with Gaussian removal and background completion using shared instance boundaries is critical to avoiding artifacts.
Rather than relying on a single 3D generative model, selecting from a multi-backend candidate pool with stability checks and orientation retries significantly improves alignment accuracy.
High-quality external mesh scans are not strictly required; surface geometry fused directly from Gaussian-rendered depth maps is sufficient for practical asset conversion.
limitations: The current pipeline assumes rigid objects and locally planar backgrounds (like tabletops); it does not handle articulated objects, deformables such as cloth, or complex non-planar hidden backgrounds.
Physical parameters like mass and friction coefficients are assigned using predefined priors rather than identified or estimated from real-world physical properties.
Orientation search retries improve geometric accuracy but roughly double the per-scene construction time (from around 35 minutes to 71 minutes).
